en: So what's an AI agent specifically? It's a
pretty broad term, but in the end, what we
typically mean with that term these days is
a system, a piece of software, you could
say, that uses a large language model as its
brain to make decisions
and that sends instructions to that model
that include your prompt, but also a lot of
extra information, for example, about tools
the model may decide to use.
But, and that's extremely important,
if the model model then makes the decision
to use a certain tool to, for example, read
a file, it's not the model that reads the
file. Instead, that decision is simply the
output of the model. It's the tokens
describing that intended tool call.
And it's then the AI agent, the piece of
software running on your system or running
somewhere in the cloud, that executes that
tool, that does open and read a file, for
example. And then that AI agent software
would For example, take the content that was
found in that file and send it back to the
model, basically telling the model, hey, I
followed your instructions, I made that tool
call, and here's what's in the file. And
then the model can make the next decision
what to do with that,
always also based on the initial prompt it
received. So if you told a model to
summarize the content of a file, it may, for
example, first make the decision to request
that read file tool call, then once it got
that response back, it may decide that it
has all the information it needs and
generate that final summary. Alternatively,
of course, if it found out that it may need
to read more files, it may request those
additional file reads.
That's what an AI agent is. It's that piece
of software which typically exposes tools to
models, which executes the requested tool
calls a model makes, and then in the end
gives the model the environment it needs to
work its way through a task so that in the
end, you as a user can use an AI agent to
get work done with help of a large language
model as a brain. That is in a nutshell what
an AI agent is.
